title: Why the cross?
hookLine: Christians explain it in several ways: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory over death

lines: WHY DID HE HAVE TO DIE?
cards: Here's a question a child might ask in church, and a very good one. If God can do anything, why did Jesus have to die? Why that way, on a Roman cross, in pain and shame?
Couldn't God just forgive? Grown-ups have asked it ever since. Surprisingly, the creeds shared across the churches never settled on one explanation.
They say he was crucified for us: that it matters, not fully how. So Christians have reached for pictures, the way several words can describe one sunrise, each catching something true.
Today's word names what the cross does.

teach.b: Atonement is an English word built from two small ones, at and one. At-one-ment: being made at one. The King James Bible uses it in Romans: "by whom we have now received the atonement."
So how does the cross make people at one with God?
Picture one: a ransom. Jesus said the Son of man came "to give his life a ransom for many." Humanity is held captive by sin and death, and Jesus pays the price to set people free.

Some early Christian writers made a great deal of this picture. Picture two: a sacrifice. Drawing on the temple and the letter to the Hebrews, Christians see Jesus as the offering that takes away sin.

In the Middle Ages, Anselm of Canterbury described Christ paying the debt of honor humanity owed God. Reformers such as Calvin, and Protestants who follow them, stress that Christ took the penalty for sin in our place.

A teacher named Abelard said the cross shows a love so great it melts our hearts and changes us. "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Picture four: victory.
Christ goes into death and breaks it open from the inside, defeating everything that holds people captive. It rings through Orthodox Easter hymns, the song of Easter morning.
Different churches lean toward different pictures, and often hold several at once.

teach.h: HEREIN IS LOVE, NOT THAT WE LOVED GOD.
teach.b: Under all of them runs one line from the first letter of John: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." Love, going all the way.

how: Christians remember the cross most of all on Good Friday, and many churches display a cross or crucifix, sing hymns about Christ's death, and remember it at every communion.

games.q: a child asks: if God can do anything, why did Jesus have to die? you're a theologian. what do the shared creeds let you say?
o: there's one official explanation, and here it is.
Christians use several pictures, each catching something true.
games.why: the shared creeds never pinned down one theory. ransom, sacrifice, example and victory each catch part of it, under one love.

practice: Let the four pictures pass slowly through your mind: a captive set free, a sacrifice for another, a love that changes you, a door broken open from the inside. Stay with the one that stirs you today.
If you pray, give thanks for what it shows you; if you don't, just stay a little longer.

wordCard.voice: Atonement. At-one-ment: being made at one with God. The name for what Christians believe the cross does.

orig.note: Greek: a ransom, the price paid to free a captive. Jesus's word in Mark 10:45.

carryVoice: Your line: love went all the way. Four pictures, one love under them. Until tomorrow.
